name: Start Small and Learn Fast
definition: Ship the smallest useful version, learn from what it does, and iterate. Shipping often beats shipping once.

rows.situation: When the plan is a six month build and then a launch
rows.under: Builds for six months, and finds out at the end.
rows.justRight: Finds the smallest version that puts the real thing in front of real users, and ships that first.
rows.over: Ships something so small it cannot teach you anything, and calls it learning.

rows.under: Moves to the next feature without reading the result.
rows.justRight: Reads what happened, changes the plan, and says what you now believe that you did not before.
rows.over: Rewrites the plan after every data point, and the direction never holds.

rows.situation: When small is used as an excuse
rows.under: Ships something broken and calls it an experiment.
rows.justRight: Keeps the scope small and the quality real. Small is about surface area, not about care.
rows.over: Polishes the small version until it costs what the full one would have.

rows.situation: When the small step is hard to undo
rows.under: Ships it fast without checking what it locks in.
rows.justRight: Asks what this makes permanent, and keeps the expensive-to-reverse parts deliberate and slow.
rows.over: Treats everything as irreversible, and loses the speed the principle exists for.

rows.situation: When the experiment did not work
rows.under: Keeps it running, because it took effort to build.
rows.justRight: Turns it off, writes down what it showed, and moves the effort.
rows.over: Kills experiments before they have run long enough to say anything.
